content:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on Tuesday sat for his confirmation hearing to make the job permanent, facing serious scrutiny from the Senate Armed Services Committee over the lack of transparency from the U.S. Navy amid President Donald Trump’s ongoing war on Iran.

Much of the grilling came from Democrats seeking clarity on mental health concerns and supply issues reported aboard aircraft carriers and on related suicide attempts by sailors amid extended deployments due to the war — but even Republican Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.) demanded some answers.

He had a different concern: the Trump administration withholding information “with regard to munitions” from Democrats who vote on how to fund the Defense Department. Rounds asked Cao, “Are you aware that on multiple occasions where there have been classified discussions, my Democrat colleagues weren’t invited?”

“And when you don’t invite our Democrat colleagues to join in on these high-end, specific, top-secret-and-above threats, that means that it limits us to basically using Republican votes only to pick up on a reconciliation,” he noted, referring to potential future supplemental defense spending bills.

Rounds continued Tuesday, “And if that doesn’t work, a supplemental would require a 60 [person] vote — which requires bipartisan support. Pretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that if they’re not even invited in to hear the information in the first place.”

Trump launched his war with the stated goal of preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons and a few additional reasons he mentioned that included some contradictions. The war has already led to the deaths of at least 23 U.S. military service members and more than 3,000 Iranians.

It also resulted in numerous sailors attempting to jump off the USS Abraham Lincoln, which had its deployment in the Middle East extended after Trump’s promises of a swift resolution in the war came crumbling down, according to Stars and Stripes and The Military Times.

Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth received widespread criticism earlier this year when reports emerged that the U.S. military had used most of its key missile interceptors in the unpopular war — and reduced its munitions stockpiles to “dangerously low” levels.

Cao was taken to task himself on Tuesday by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) over his August statement that journalists who reported on the struggling Navy sailors were “trying to paint” America’s “warriors as victims” — and for calling their attempted suicides “mitigations.”

Rounds stayed focused on transparency, telling Cao, “Now, we’ve talked about this before.”

“I don’t recall that you were necessarily in those meetings or not, but I want a commitment from you, and we’ll ask it from others, that we move this back to a bipartisan basis when it comes to sharing critical information in the defense of this country,” he told Cao.

Rounds noted this “requires a cooperative effort on your part in the future.”

Cao responded swiftly, “Senator, if confirmed, I commit to being open and honest with the entire Senate and the Congress also.”

“I mean, this is a bipartisan issue,” Cao continued. “National defense is not a partisan issue. This is a bipartisan issue. And so I give you my commitment that I will work with both sides, just like I have bringing [congressional delegations] onboard [Navy ships].”

“I’m open and honest and I, I pledge that I’ll work with both sides,” he concluded.
